title: The death of cool America - and the cringe that killed it
text:
The death of cool America - and the cringe that killed it

 'It seems the rest of the world is pushing back against America’s cultural might,' writes Tufayel Ahmed (Inset photo: Bruce Yuanyue Bi via Getty) 

# The death of cool America – and the cringe that killed it

 We were all, at some point, captivated by the 'American Dream'. No longer 

 June 08, 2026 6:00 am (Updated 12:01 pm) 

 

 Tufayel Ahmed Culture and entertainment journalist 

> Welcome to Trump’s America, The i Paper’s World Insight series presenting the sharpest, deepest thinking on an era-defining shift in history and politics, investigating how Donald Trump and his administration have changed the US and the world – and where we go from here.
> 
> • How America’s conspiracy theorists broke the US • The US is becoming impossible to live in • I told Trump over dinner he didn’t have my loyalty – it sealed my fate • This is how the world will look after Trump • Sin City has lost its shine. It shows how far America has fallen • The influencer who turned on Maga – claiming it has a dark secret • Inside America’s most loyal Trump town – where people still think he’s ‘a good man’

A UFC cage on the lawn of the White House to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States. It is so tacky that Aaron Sorkin, arguably one of Hollywood’s best screenwriters, couldn’t dream it if he tried. But that is the very real state of affairs under Donald Trump, the President who has single-handedly made America, well, decidedly uncool.

There was a time every girl around the world wanted to emulate “The Rachel”, Jennifer Aniston’s layered, shoulder-length bob haircut from Friends, and American exports from Steven Spielberg to Cindy Crawford and Michael Jackson to Muhammad Ali seemed like the coolest people on the planet. Name a millennial journalist who didn’t envy Carrie Bradshaw’s $4-per-word rate to write for Vogue and main character energy. I’d hazard we were all, at some point, captivated by the “American Dream”.

Not so in Trump’s America, which, in his second term, is a decidedly more vulgar place – a place where, yes, let’s have UFC cage fighting on the front lawn of the presidential abode, because why not? He’s already proposed an Arc de Trump, a $400m White House ballroom and attempted to rename the Kennedy Center. The cage-fighting match is but the latest example of America’s cultural decay, which is increasingly leaning towards the 1 per cent. An America where billionaire WAGs are able to buy their way into Anna Wintour’s periphery and billion-dollar mergers can seemingly end a venerated American institution like The Late Show with little resistance.

Experts found a rapid rise in autism diagnoses among 16-to 20-year-olds since 2010 in the UK, as well as a rise in women and white people, compared to other ethnicities.

## What were the findings?

- Researchers from the Medical Research Council looked at data from the UK and Sweden.
- They found that new diagnoses have increased from six people per 100,000 in 2010, to 64 per 100,000 in 2023. 
- Analysis also showed there has been a change in the make-up of people diagnosed with autism, with a decrease in those with a prior diagnosis of epilepsy.
- Instead, they found an increase in the proportion of people who had a prior diagnosis of ADHD, stress-related disorders, eating disorders, headaches and chronic fatigue.

## The story in numbers

58%

The proportion of autism diagnoses in people with anxiety more than doubled form 29 per cent to 58 per cent between 2010 and 2023.

- In the UK, 24.5 million adults contributed to the study, including 141,119 with an autism diagnosis.
- Writing in BMJ Mental Health, the team said this could be the result of “greater appreciation of nuanced forms of autism that may have previously been labelled as other conditions due to overlapping features, particularly in females”. 

Half of women in the perimenopause or menopause say their career has suffered as a result, with workers cutting their hours or feeling forced to turn down opportunities for career progression, according to a new survey.

## Lack of support for symptoms

Nearly one in three said their life stage had influenced their retirement savings, according to the research for Scottish Widows. A similar number also said their regular finances had been affected.

And 50 per cent of women surveyed said they would like more support at work. 17 per cent said they had been forced to take time away to manage symptoms.

- One in eight (13 per cent) women had reduced their working hours and 10 per cent had turned down a promotion or career progression opportunity, for menopause-related reasons.
- Scottish Widows found that a 50-year-old woman in full-time work taking a six-month unpaid break could potentially cost £1,300 in pension contributions.
- Gaps in pension contributions will have a bigger impact over time, as savers will also miss out on the interest that could have been earned on them.
- Two-thirds of women surveyed believe employers should be required to provide better support to women experiencing menopause symptoms, including financial support.

 The i Paper takes a look at why the bill for pensions keeps rising on both sides of the Channel – and what can be done about it.

France will be unable to resolve its debt crisis without tackling sky-high pension bills, economists have warned. It spends a massive 14 per cent of its GDP on pensions and the costs are rising every day. Falling birth rates and rising life expectancy in France and the UK means pensions are mounting pressure on public finances.

Heidi Karjalainen, senior research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, says bigger private pension pots in the UK are making it easier to increase the state pension age, whereas “in France, it’s been really difficult to do that”.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey have been planning the Budget for months (Photo: Ian Forsyth/Getty Images)

French President Emmanuel Macron speaks following a videoconference with G7 leaders (Photo: AFP)

It’s this cushion that will help the UK better navigate the trials and tribulations that come with an ageing population and falling birth rates, she says.

The French proposals were announced “without much notice”, Karjalainen noted, while the UK made the decision more than a decade ago. Thorne says France offers a “pointed lesson in what can happen when governments try to reset the terms of the pension contract: five prime ministers in two years; mass street protests; and a reform ultimately diluted by political reality even when the economics were clear”.

“America spent decades being the world’s dream factory, the place that set the agenda for TV, music, film, and the mainstream cultural conversation. What’s changed isn’t the output – it’s the attitude,” says Dan Wakeford, founder of the Celebrity Intelligence newsletter and former editor-in-chief of popular US magazines People and Us Weekly (where I work as London editor). “When culture becomes a vehicle for brand dominance and political posturing rather than genuine expression, the rest of the world notices. Cool has always been about freedom and edge, and that has been lost in America.”

While there remained pockets of cultural rebellion during Trump’s first term – Donald Glover as Childish Gambino’s searing “This Is America”, for one, and America’s de facto sovereign Taylor Swift making her first public political endorsement – this time there is a consensus that Americans have laid down their swords and rolled over. “The irony is that American culture becomes most influential when it’s in opposition to power, not in service of it,” says Wakeford. “Punk, hip-hop, indie film, the golden age of TV – all of it came from the margins pushing back.”

Now, it seems, the rest of the world is pushing back against America’s cultural might. A March YouGov poll found that 68 per cent of Brits see the US as having a mostly or entirely negative impact on the world. A 2023 YouGov poll found that the majority of adults in the nine countries surveyed deemed America to have too much or a significant influence on national culture.

In the UK, 83 per cent of respondents said they felt that way about America’s effect on film, 77 per cent thought the same of television and 60 per cent said the same of music.

Film was once synonymous with Hollywood and dominated our cinemas, but more and more, home-grown is winning out. In India, Bollywood and the Telugu film industries are thriving, while the world’s highest-grossing film of 2025 – family animation Ne Zha 2 – came from China. It’s $2.2bn haul is a number that the likes of Disney and Paramount, the latter recently acquired by Trump-allied billionaire Larry Ellison and his son David, must look at with more than a hint of jealousy.

Disney’s new Star Wars entry, The Mandalorian and Grogu, has struggled at the worldwide box office as even the most ardent fans of a galaxy far, far away seem to be put off by constant CGI-laden sequels and spin-offs that seem designed less with quality in mind than profiteering. It’s telling, too, that the top two movies at the US box office last weekend – Backrooms and Obsession – were two low-budget horror films by little-known directors making their theatrical debuts. It suggests that like the rest of us, Americans are no longer lured by inoffensive movies designed to appeal to every demographic – so-called four-quadrant, green-screen slop – and crave more originality.

While British sporting culture has largely been free of Americanisation (no Tyson Fury boxing match in the grounds of Buckingham Palace or Downing Street – yet), the bastion that is our national sport, football, is seeing its boundaries tested. The news that the 2026 FIFA World Cup final will host a Super Bowl-esque half-time show starring Madonna, BTS and Shakira was met with the collective eye-rolling of the rest of the world, not least because of the sanctity with which fans treat the game.

“The half-time show in the final is an insult to real supporters and actually the players involved,” says Duncan Wright, creative lead at Press Box PR and former sports journalist. “The normal 15-minute break will now be double – and that can change completely the way the match is being played.”

While FIFA is billing the World Cup half-time show as an act of philanthropy (it will apparently support a charitable effort to raise $100m for children’s education), many see it for what it is: further undue American influence on a global stage. “Importing the Super Bowl template into a sport that belongs to the entire planet feels less like a gift and more like a hostile takeover that nobody asked for,” says Wakeford.

It remains to be seen whether those within the football industry and aficionados alike revolt against the imposition of a grandiose Americanised spectacle, but the divisive reaction to this year’s Met Gala, the fashion event of the year, may forecast the reception that awaits. 

“How the Met Gala Transformed Into the Tacky ‘Bezos Ball,’” Variety wrote of this year’s extravaganza, which saw an injection of billionaire bucks in exchange for Jeff Bezos and wife Lauren Sánchez being named honorary co-chairs. Admission to the ball was once a money-can’t-buy ticket, reliant on meritocracy, fashion credentials and popularity within the zeitgeist. Now, billionaires can purchase a seat at the cool table alongside Beyoncé and Nicole Kidman – incidentally, making institutions such as the Met Gala considerably less cool.

“I stayed home because this year, the illusion cracked beyond repair,” writes former Vogue editor Gabriella Karefa-Johnson, who hosted the alternative Ball Without Billionaires instead of attending this year’s event. Fashion “does not originate in the highest C-suites and penthouses and filter into the street” but “rises from the people,” she argues.

Indeed, culture itself is not dictated by the elite
